In mathematics, '''André planes''' are a class of finite [[translation plane]]s found by André.<ref>{{Citation | last1=André | first1=Johannes | title=Über nicht-Desarguessche Ebenen mit transitiver Translationsgruppe | url=http://resolver.sub.uni-goettingen.de/purl?GDZPPN002384345 | doi=10.1007/BF01187370 | mr=0063056 | year=1954 | journal=[[Mathematische Zeitschrift]] | issn=0025-5874 | volume=60 | pages=156–186| s2cid=123661471 }}</ref> The [[Desarguesian plane]] and the [[Hall plane]]s are examples of André planes; the two-dimensional regular [[Near-field (mathematics)|nearfield]] planes are also André planes.

==Construction==
Let <math>F = GF(q)</math> be a finite [[Field (mathematics)|field]], and let <math>K = GF(q^n)</math> be a degree <math>n</math> [[field extension|extension field]] of <math>F</math>. Let <math>\Gamma</math> be the group of [[field automorphism]]s of <math>K</math> over <math>F</math>, and let <math>\beta</math> be an arbitrary mapping from <math>F</math> to <math>\Gamma</math> such that <math>\beta(1)=1</math>. Finally, let <math>N</math> be the [[Field norm|norm]] function from <math>K</math> to <math>F</math>.

Define a quasifield <math>Q</math> with the same elements and addition as K, but with multiplication defined via <math>a \circ b = a^{\beta(N(b))} \cdot b</math>, where <math>\cdot</math> denotes the normal field multiplication in <math>K</math>. Using this [[quasifield]] to [[Translation plane#Algebraic Construction with Coordinates|construct a plane]] yields an André plane.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Weibel | first1=Charles |author-link=Charles Weibel | title=Survey of Non-Desarguesian Planes  | url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200710/ | year=2007 | journal= Notices of the AMS  | volume= 54 | issue=10 | pages=1294–1303}}</ref>

==Properties==
# André planes exist for all proper prime powers <math>p^n</math> with <math>p</math> prime and <math>n</math> a positive [[integer]] greater than one.
# Non-Desarguesian André planes exist for all proper prime powers except for <math>2^n</math> where <math>n</math> is prime.

==Small examples==
For planes of order 25 and below, classification of Andrè planes is a consequence of either theoretical calculations or computer searches which have determined all translation planes of a given order:

* The smallest non-Desarguesian André plane has order 9, and it is isomorphic to the [[Hall plane#The Hall plane of order 9|Hall plane]] of that order.
* The translation planes of order 16 have all been classified, and again the only non-Desarguesian André plane is the [[Hall plane]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Projective Planes of Order 16|url=http://ericmoorhouse.org/pub/planes16/|access-date=2020-11-08|website=ericmoorhouse.org}}</ref>
* There are three non-Desarguesian André planes of order 25.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Chen | first1=G. | title=The complete classification of the non-Desarguesian André planes of order 25 | date=1994 | journal=Journal of South China Normal University | volume=3 | pages=122–127}}</ref> These are the [[Hall plane]], the regular [[Near-field (mathematics)|nearfield]] plane, and a third plane not constructible by other techniques.<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Dover|first=Jeremy M.|date=2019-02-27|title=A genealogy of the translation planes of order 25|class=math.CO|eprint=1902.07838}}</ref>
* There is a single non-Desarguesian André plane of order 27.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Projective Planes of Order 27|url=http://ericmoorhouse.org/pub/planes27/|access-date=2020-11-08|website=ericmoorhouse.org}}</ref>

Enumeration of Andrè planes specifically has been performed for other small orders:<ref>{{cite arXiv|last=Dover|first=Jeremy M.|date=2021-05-16|title=Computational Enumeration of Andrè Planes|class=math.CO|eprint=2105.07439}}</ref>
